_source: mixed-mode .NET binary using hidapi. The transport and the command table
are read directly out of the shipped code -- hts_send_cmd's IL and the
HTS_*_CMD static byte arrays -- so they are observed, not guessed.
What is still unconfirmed is marked with _needsVerification on the field:
the raw<->friendly value maps (which byte means 4000 Hz), because those
live in WinForms UI code rather than in the command table. Read them off
your own mouse with `hskctl get <field>` while the vendor app shows you
the real value, then fill in `values` and set status to verified.
status: partial means hskctl will talk to the device but you should
sanity-check every reading before trusting a write.

match._comment: VID and PIDs are the constants hts_init matches on. The config endpoint is identified by a vendor usage page (0xffff observed) plus a feature report -- not by interface number, which was 7 on the dongle despite the driver's 'mi_02' string.

transport._comment: hts_send_cmd: Sleep(60); hid_send_feature_report(h, tx, 65); Sleep(60); hid_get_feature_report(h, rx, 65); accept iff rx[1] == 0xA1. Byte 0 is the hidapi report-id byte and is 0 (unnumbered reports). No checksum anywhere in the command table.
transport._linkProbeComment: Byte 4 says which transport the packet is addressed over -- it is a property of the endpoint you opened, NOT of where the mouse currently is. The `connection` reply answers a different question (is the mouse linked over RF or sitting on the cable), and using it to pick byte 4 breaks the moment those disagree: plug the cable in while the dongle is still in, connection reports 0, every packet then goes to the dongle with the wrong flag, and the firmware ACKs and ignores all of it -- so every field reads 0 and nothing says why. Instead, probe: send this read on each flag and keep whichever answers with a payload that is not all zeros. dpi is the right probe because a working mouse cannot have an all-zero DPI block, whereas battery, motion sync and angle snap can all legitimately read 0.

commands._comment: Byte 2 is the payload length, byte 3 the opcode, byte 4 the link flag, byte 5 onwards the value. The read opcode is always the write opcode + 0x80. Commands whose opcode already has the high bit set are read-only.
commands._dpiComment: ONE write, not two. hts_set_get_dpis_colors (7 bytes per stage: X u16be, Y u16be, R G B) and hts_set_get_dpis_colors_O (5 bytes per stage, no separate Y) are selected by globe_FW_Old_New_Flag -- new firmware uses the first, old firmware the second. They are alternatives, never a sequence. Firmware 1.0.7 reports separate X and Y, so it is the new path. Sending the legacy packet to new firmware misaligns every stage from byte 9 on and writes colour bytes into the Y axis.

dpi._settleComment: 51 bytes of payload, against one for the scalar commands. At the vendor's 60ms the reply is sometimes not ready, which arrives as an all-zero payload and looks exactly like a command the mouse ignored -- so selecting a stage from the panel failed intermittently while the smaller commands were fine.

repairOnWrite.why: stage count of 0 makes the firmware write no stages at all

dpi._repairComment: rx[6] is the DPI stage count, and the firmware writes that many stages out of the packet. Read-modify-write copies it back verbatim, so a mouse reporting 0 -- as this one did, almost certainly zeroed by the legacy-packet incident -- discards every DPI value and every stage colour, restores the 0, and does it again next time. The active-stage byte beside it keeps working because it sits outside the array, which is exactly how the bug hid. Confirmed on hardware 2026-08-18: setting the count to 7 made both value and colour writes land immediately.

commands._sleepComment: Sleep is a sub-command of opcode 0x02: byte 6 selects 0x07 to set or 0x87 to get, and the value is a big-endian u16 at bytes 7-8.
commands._resetComment: HTS_RESET_CMD restores factory defaults. Deliberately not wired to any field -- nothing in the panel should be one keystroke away from wiping the mouse's config.
commands._linkFlagComment: linkFlag:false marks commands whose vendor function never sets byte 4. For sleep that byte carries part of the sub-command, so writing a link flag into it corrupts the packet.
commands._replyComment: The reply echoes the request: rx[2]=response length, rx[3]=opcode, rx[4]=link flag, payload from rx[5]. Crucially the firmware ACKs a packet carrying the wrong link flag and then ignores it, replying with an all-zero payload -- so an ACK is not proof of success.

charging._note: Read out of hts_get_battery + battery_update_ui: the reply carries two bytes, rx[5] and rx[6]. The app assigns rx[6] to b_percent and shows the charging label when rx[5] > 0. So the offsets are decoded, not guessed.
charging._needsVerification: still observed 0 on the cable -- if it never reads non-zero, the endpoint being answered is the dongle rather than the mouse, not a wrong offset

connection._note: observed 1 on the dongle; the cable reports 0

pollingRate._note: Every value here was measured by timing the mouse's own input reports -- none inferred. The register is NOT a single formula: raw 1..6 divide a 1000 Hz base, while raw 32 and 64 are high-rate codes clocking 2000 and 4000 Hz. Non-monotonic, so an explicit map is the only honest model. Raw 8 (predicted 125 Hz) and raw 16 are untested.

liftOffDistance._note: Read out of hts_liftoff_low_radioButton_CheckedChanged: the low button sets 1, the high button sets 2. The earlier 0/1 map was wrong in both directions -- writing '1mm' sent raw 0, which the firmware rejected, and a mouse sitting at raw 1 (actually 1mm) was displayed as 2mm.

debounceMs._needsVerification: read returns byte 0 of a 4-byte tuple (observed 03 0a 23 14, row 1 of the driver's 6-row table) while the write takes a row index -- the two are not the same number, so writing is disabled until the table is modelled

sleepMinutes._needsVerification: observed 240 on hardware; the unit is not established. If minutes it would be 4 hours, if seconds 4 minutes -- do not present it as either until measured.

activeDpiStage._note: rx[5]. hts_set_get_dpis_colors reads it into the struct field the level combo clamps, so it is the currently selected stage.

dpiStageCount._note: rx[6] -- how many DPI stages the mouse cycles through, not an unknown flag. hts_set_get_dpis_colors writes tx[6] from the struct field that hts_dpi_level_combo_SelectionChangeCommitted sets from the 'DPI level' combo, and that handler clamps the active stage down to it. Reads 0 on this mouse, which is odd -- it cycles more stages than that -- so either the firmware does not use it the way the app does, or an earlier bad packet zeroed it.
dpiStageCount._needsVerification: writing it is untested on hardware; read it, change the count, and check the mouse cycles that many stages before trusting the write

dpiStage1._note: X axis of stage 1. Writing it also writes the Y axis in the same packet, matching the vendor app, which keeps the axes equal unless XY_DPI_Enable is ticked. Set dpiStage1Y on its own for an independent Y.

dpiStage1Y._note: Y axis of stage 1. Writing this alone leaves X, so the axes can be set independently; writing X re-links them.

_pollingNote: Resolved. The vendor slider emits 1<<position, so positions 0..6 give raw 1,2,4,8,16,32,64. Measured: 1=1000, 2=500, 4=250, 32=2000, 64=4000 Hz. 4K is reachable and needs no separate mode.
